item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Aber Kawas becomes first Palestinian American elected to New York State Legislature
item.description:
Aber Kawas becomes first Palestinian American elected to New York State Legislature

Submitted by Mounira Elsamra on Tue, 11/03/2026 - 20:41
Kawas is also the first 'hijabi' to be elected to office in the state legislature
Left to right: Diana Moreno, David Orkin, Samantha Kattan, Aber Kawas and Claire Valdez raise their hands during a primary-night watch party at 99 Scott Studio on 23 June 2026 in the East Williamsburg neighbourhood of New York City (Michael M Santiago/Getty Images via AFP)
Off

Aber Kawas has won her bid for the New York State Senate District 12 seat, taking a 75 percent share of the votes with 90 percent of the votes counted when the race was called by the New York Times. 

Kawas has made history as the first hijab-wearing Palestinian American to serve in the New York State Legislature. She joins a small list of Palestinian Americans to ever be elected at the state level across the US. 

Kawas posted a short message to X after the victory saying, "We made history". 

"Fund dignity, fight destruction" was the slogan Kawas campaigned with. "Fund dignity" refers to her stance on healthcare for all, fast and reliable public transportation, and affordable housing. "Fight destruction" refers to her positions on stopping climate change, protecting immigrants and her "No money for war" stance.

Kawas is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, a group that has made unprecedented gains since its member Zohran Mamdani won the historic mayoral race in New York City last year. 

She was among the growing slate of Democratic Socialists of America candidates that ran in this cycle.

Many progressive Democrats endorsed Kawas, including Mamdani, Senator Bernie Sanders, and Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib.

Her win reflects the growing footprint of the pro-Palestine community within the US political landscape. 

'Not On Our Dime'

Before entering politics, Kawas spent more than 15 years as an organiser fighting for workers' rights, immigrant communities, and Palestinian rights. 

Last month, Kawas told Middle East Eye that in 2023 she was part of a coalition of activists looking to work at a local level of government to disrupt funding that supports the Israeli state and its military occupation of Palestine.

They discovered several charities in the US that had raised millions of dollars to send Jewish Americans to the occupied West Bank as settlers on Palestinian land in violation of international law. 

Kawas helped develop and launch the "Not On Our Dime" campaign, which seeks to prohibit New York nonprofits from funding organisations that support Israel's illegal occupation of the Palestinian territories.

"It shouldn't be allowed in New York state law for a group that is registered as a charity organisation - which should be collecting money to help people - to take that money and commit human rights atrocities," Kawas told MEE. 

To introduce the bill, she worked with Mamdani, then a New York City Assembly member, and State Senator Jabari Brisport, who sponsored and authored the bill in May 2023. 

But due to strong opposition from lawmakers, the legislation titled "Ending New York funding of Israeli settler violence act" never became a law. 

"It was interesting to work with then-Assembly member Mamdani because I was sceptical of politicians," Kawas told MEE, explaining that this process and bill inspired her.

"It was interesting to work with him as an elected official and see how he could use that position to do something that was unprecedented.

"When we had introduced the Not On Our Dime bill, that had never been done before in New York State; nobody had ever proactively introduced something that was fighting for Palestinian human rights," she said.

End collaboration with ICE

Kawas was born and raised in Brooklyn to Palestinian parents who immigrated to the US in the 1990s. She said despite her parents being undocumented at the time, she felt accepted in her community. But that sense of safety shifted when Kawas was in the fourth grade, following the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks.

She described how fear in the New York Muslim community of being surveilled, deported or facing unfounded terror charges was pervasive. Even in elementary school, her classmates began to distance themselves from her. 

As a child of immigrants, Kawas takes a pro-immigration stance and vows to end New York's collaboration with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) by passing the New York For All Act, which would prohibit the state and local agencies from cooperating with federal civil immigration enforcement.

"I think it's really important to talk about the idea that it destroys entire lives and families. It's not just the one person - oftentimes you will see a story, and the story is two people got picked up by ICE, or one person gets picked up by ICE off the street, and that one person has an entire family around them," she said.

Kawas knows all too well the effects of having a family member deported or detained. Her father was deported to Jordan when she was in high school. Kawas explained to MEE how her dad's detention and ultimate deportation affected her family. 

"Having someone taken out of a family unit, in many ways, shifts everything. It shifts our lives economically. We weren't able to have as much money, afford the same things," she said. 

"Every one of my siblings had to work from a really young age to be able to help my mom afford to take care of us. That's an economic shift and a psychological shift." 

Palestinian activism 

Kawas is challenging the status quo of "Progressive except for Palestine" politics. Before the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023 and the subsequent genocide in Gaza, when she spoke to elected Democrats about Palestine-related human rights issues, she got little response. 

"People believed that to have a political career, you couldn't speak for Palestinian human rights, that you could never speak out against the state of Israel; that would be political suicide," she told MEE. 

While campaigning, she has not shied away from her Palestinian identity. Earlier this year, she was arrested for protesting against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's arrival in New York City at the United Nations General Assembly, where she was among dozens arrested, and later released.

"It felt really meaningful to participate in civil disobedience with other elected officials and politicians," Kawas said. 

"I grew up in a time period where you just never had an elected official stand up for Palestinian human rights. So, to be amongst the ten or more politicians, at that moment I thought it was really cool. I wish we could have done more. I really wish that Netanyahu never entered the city." 

Earlier this month, she voiced opposition to a $750,000 deal between the New York Police Department (NYPD) and Israeli surveillance company Cognyte to develop AI-powered mobile phone tracking.

"This powerful tool violates the rights of all New Yorkers, giving the police greater ability to track our phones and access sensitive data with little transparency or oversight," Kawas wrote on X.

"However, this is about more than just one company or contract. The NYPD has a long history of mass surveillance of Muslim communities, Palestine solidarity activists, and communities of colour, and police departments across the state are sharing AI surveillance data with ICE to aid in the deportation of our immigrant neighbours." 

Last week, the NYPD backed out of the deal, following backlash from civil rights groups.

As a Palestinian who is unabashedly vocal on Palestine, Kawas is the embodiment of shifting political tides. 

"New Yorkers are asking for a change in the administration. We are actually really hopeful that we have a system of community safety that is actually interested in people's lives and not interested in continuing these patterns of policing that are violent and that are affecting so many New Yorkers," she said.

item.description:
US midterm elections 2026: Democrats sweep House and Senate in major rebuke to Trump

Submitted by Yasmine El-Sabawi on Tue, 11/03/2026 - 18:19
Democrats flip South Carolina senate seat and Texas governorship
Supporters of Democratic US Senate candidate Adam Hamilton celebrate during an election-night watch party at the Marriott Kansas City Overland Park on 3 November 2026 in Overland Park, Kansas (Jim Vondruska/Getty Images/AFP)
Off

The Democrats wrested control of the US Senate and the House of Representatives from Republicans, in a major rebuke of President Donald Trump's policy agenda. 

In the lower chamber of Congress, known as the House, Democrats gained 25 seats. A party needs at least 218 seats to control the House.

By early Wednesday, Democrats secured 220 seats and were on track for a comfortable majority as more races are called. 

The speakership of the House is likely to go to the first Black lawmaker to take the post, New York Congressman Hakeem Jeffries. 

In the Senate, where only a third of the 100 seats were contested, Democrats picked up at least seven seats, giving them a 53 seat majority. 

They can now block Trump's judicial nominees as well as funding for the US-Israeli war on Iran. (More details here on the difference between whether it's a simple majority or a gain of more than five seats). 

As the results poured in, Trump took to social media to distance himself from Republican candidates, despite campaigning heavily for them. 

"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump wrote on X. 

In an interview with the Wall Street Journal, Trump said that the Iran war was partially to blame for the Democrats sweeping victory. "Iran was a piece of it," he said. 

US midterm elections 2026: Abdul El-Sayed becomes first Muslim elected to Senate
Read More »

Jeffries hailed the results as a "red, white and blue moment" in American history, saying the Democrats will deliver "dramatic change". 

Jeffries focused on affordability, rising prices and allegations of corruption among Trump's family and political allies, but notably he did not mention the US-Israeli war on Iran in his speech. 

"This is not a partisan moment. This is a patriotic one. This is not a blue moment or a red moment. It’s a red, white and blue moment because America has won tonight," he said. 

Still, Iran was quick to label the Democrats' electoral sweep as a repudiation of the war. 

"Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran's parliament wrote on X. 

"If the US government betrays the will of its people to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn that our NO comes with a nightmare," he added.

This midterm election cycle was the most expensive of all time, with total spending reaching $11.6bn, according to Ad Impact. 

A Senate sweep

Pro-Israel lobbying groups alone paid out some $40m in support of candidates who ran against progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, both in the primary and the general election. 

El-Sayed declared victory early on Wednesday, with 80 percent of the votes counted, showing him in a comfortable 51.8 percent lead compared to his Republican opponent Mike Rogers at 46.2 percent.

In a stunning and symbolic turn, the Democrats flipped a South Carolina Senate seat that was once held by Lindsey Graham. 

Can a Democrat-controlled Senate thwart Trump's agenda?
Read More »

Maine's Republican Senator Susan Collins was ousted from office after 30 years in an upset win by Democrat Troy Jackson. 

Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Graham's sister, Darline, to take the seat of the deceased senator who championed the war on Iran and Ukraine. Darline was endorsed by Trump. 

In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton defeated incumbent Republican Roger Marshall, making him the first Democrat to win the Kansas seat in almost 100 years. 

In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek defeated his Republican rival Ashley Hinson in an unexpected victory. 

In deep Republican-red Texas, Trump-backed, scandal-plagued Ken Paxton lost to Democrat James Talarico, flipping a seat held by Republicans for more than 30 years. 

Talarico has endeared himself to Texans by highlighting his strong attachment to his Christian faith and also his support for Israel, while at the same time saying there should be conditions on the weapons the US sends there. 

Paxton was previously indicted for fraud and also impeached for corruption while in the state legislature, but never convicted. As Texas attorney general, he has been at the forefront of efforts to criminalise the country's largest Muslim civil rights organisation. 

The House

An incoming contingent of younger progressives from deep-blue districts are all now headed to Congress. There are now enough of them to potentially delay or derail plans by more centrist Democrats in the House. 

They are largely political novices who carried the winning messages of the Zohran Mamdani campaign for mayor in New York City: a focus on affordability for working people and support for Palestinian rights.

They have also refused to accept corporate money to fund their campaigns - a relatively risky move in a country where elections can be wholly decided on how much money a candidate has raised. 

Adam Hamawy, an Egyptian-American surgeon who gained national attention for his harrowing 2024 medical mission to Gaza, won New Jersey’s 12th district. 

Ilhan Omar was never supposed to be an equal
Read More »

Next door in New York, Darializa Avila Chevalier, a Democratic Socialist who mounted a stunning upset when she defeated an incumbent in the state's 13th District earlier this year; state legislator Claire Valdez, also a Democratic Socialist who won the primary for the 7th District; and Brad Lander, a prominent Mamdani ally and former comptroller for New York City who won the primary for the 10th District, are all headed to Washington, DC, next year. 

In Pennsylvania's 3rd District, progressive Democrat and state legislator Chris Rabb is also headed to Congress, as is 29-year-old Ethiopian immigrant Melat Kiros in Colorado's 1st District. 

Fewer than two dozen House seats across the country were considered toss-ups this year based on the polling and voter sentiment in the days just before the election.

Of the three Republicans who ran in districts that Democratic presidential contender Kamala Harris won in 2024, New York 17th District Congressman Mike Lawler was most at risk.

So much so that Trump appeared to have summoned some anti-Zionist Jewish leaders from that district to the White House in a bid to rally support for Lawler, given their outsized influence. 

Lawler conceded the race on Tuesday night. 

Other toss-up races went the Democrats ways, contributing to their majority in the House. 

In Colorado's 8th district, Democrat Manny Rutinel defeated Republican incumbent Gabe Evans, according to CBS projections. 

Democrats take Texas Governorship

In a stunning upset that underscored the extent of the Democrat's sweep Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governorship, ousting Greg Abbott after three terms. Texas is the most populous Republican state and a bastion of the party's power. 

In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy for governor, making her the first Democrat to win the seat since 2006. 

The US midterm elections, particularly the first ones in a new president's term, are always seen as a referendum on the White House's conduct. Trump launched a war on Iran, alongside Israel, that has upended the entire region and skyrocketed fuel prices for Americans. 

Only three in 10 Americans now approve of Trump's conduct during his first two years, Pew Research revealed last month. 

Aber Kawas becomes first Palestinian American elected to New York State Legislature
Read More »

Every two years, all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and about a third of the 100-seat Senate are contested. Representatives serve two-year terms, while senators, who have a more senior role and are generally more prominent faces, serve six-year terms.

Voter turnout suggested intense dissapointment within Trump's base and an energized Democratic electorate.

The biggest increases in votes cast compared to the 2022 midterms came in places that former Vice President Kamala Harris won handily in 2024, according to data from Politico. Turnout was up 15 percent in counties Harris won by at least 70 percent in 2024, compared to just 7 percent in counties Trump won by 70 percent or more.  

For immigrants, and Arab and Muslim Americans in particular, the stakes were uncommonly high, as the administration cracks down on noncitizens, punishes criticism of Israel and pro-Palestine sentiment, and employs open, anti-Muslim verbiage - all moves that have dominated national headlines and radically reshaped how many minority communities go about their daily lives.

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) played an especially active role in races, but their influence appeared diminished. In fact, in Michigan, early exit polling showed that El-Sayed received 60 percent of the votes from Jewish Americans who cast ballots before Election Day. 

Each state has two senators, regardless of size or population. House seats, however, are based on population distribution. There are no term limits.

The 120th Congress will be sworn in on 3 January 2027.

item.description:
US midterm elections 2026: Abdul El-Sayed becomes first Muslim elected to Senate

Submitted by Yasmine El-Sabawi on Tue, 11/03/2026 - 17:11
Egyptian-American Democrat condemns use of US tax dollars to support Israeli 'apartheid and genocidal war' in historic victory speech
Democratic US Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed speaks onstage after declaring victory in Michigan's US Senate race during an election night party at The Department at Hudson's in Detroit, Michigan, early on 4 November 2026 (Jeff Kowalsky/AFP)
Off

Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won a highly coveted Michigan Senate seat on Wednesday, and will become the first Muslim to serve in the upper chamber of Congress come January. 

El-Sayed declared victory with 80 percent of votes counted, showing him in a comfortable 51.8 percent lead compared to his Republican opponent Mike Rogers at 46.2 percent.

The Associated Press declared El-Sayed the winner at 2:27 am EST (7:27 GMT)

"I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect," Sayed said in an energized victory speech, where he said he was able to overcome Islamophobic slurs aimed at him by US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.

"To all the parents who struggled to explain [to their kids] why the president openly mocked someone for their name or how they pray, let them know tomorrow that the bad guys lost," he said to cheers and applause. 

"They want an America that is too small for some of us. We know that America is big enough for all of us," he added. 

US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed celebrated his victory by taking on Aipac and the special interests that poured millions into trying to defeat him https://t.co/Wd2L9m9qdC

— Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye) November 4, 2026

Sayed, smiling and responding to lively applause specifically called out Vance and Trump. 

"JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January," he said. 

To Trump he said: "Donald, I know you struggle with my name, so after JD swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me Senator". 

Sayed's victory marks a watershed moment in US political history. 

'We don't want our money sent to do apartheid or genocidal war,'

Abdul El-Sayed

A progressive who shocked the party establishment when he narrowly defeated Haley Stevens, who was backed by pro-Israel lobbying groups, in the August Democratic primary, Sayed was endorsed early by the Senate's leading voice on progressive issues, Bernie Sanders of Vermont. 

Sayed specifically challenged the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) and other pro-Israel lobbying groups that spent tens of millions of dollars against him. 

"To Aipac who spent $42 million against us. Thank you for giving me the opportunity to beat you twice," he said. 

"They try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars," he said. "If you believe in equal rights for peace, diginity and self-determination that's not hate, it's love," he said. 

"We want our taxes spent here...we don't want our money sent to do apartheid or genocidal war," he said. 

That race proved so pivotal that half a million more Democratic voters showed up to the polls than in previous primary races, which typically see low turnouts, Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said at the time. 

In the later stages of his campaign, Sayed received the backing of former President Barack Obama, who remains one of the most popular figures among the party establishment. 

Who is Abdul El-Sayed?

The 42-year-old's full name is Abdulrahman Mohammed El-Sayed. He is married to an Indian-American doctor and has two daughters. When he graduated from the University of Michigan and gave the commencement address in 2007, the event's keynote speaker, former President Bill Clinton, praised his oratory skills at the podium. 

The Michigan native then earned a medical degree from Columbia University and led the public health departments in Detroit and Wayne County before launching what was seen as a long-shot bid for the US Senate in 2025.

But it wasn't his first time.

In 2018, Sayed unsuccessfully sought the governorship of Michigan, but he managed to lay the foundations for his vision for Medicare-For-All: the establishment of a national health insurance programme in the US.

As private insurance premiums have skyrocketed in the US since then, that policy proposal grew increasingly popular among those on the left and the right, as did Sayed's criticism of the closeness of the US-Israel relationship - an approach that was very similar to that of the highly popular New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani. 

Sayed has repeatedly said that he has never met with corporate lobbyists, and in both his campaigns, he raised money only from individual donors rather than corporations. 

'He's different'

Unlike Mamdani, however, Sayed was not endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, as he sought the support of his party's centrists in a volatile swing state like Michigan. 

He appeared on as many television networks, podcasts, and social media influencer accounts as he could, in a bid to reach as many segments of the American public as possible, regardless of political affiliation, Sayed often said. 

But he was also met with such a disproportionate amount of media scrutiny that he inadvertently became better known - and perhaps more appealing - to voters than his opponent, former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers.

Rogers, who was not under the microscope in the same manner, was endorsed by President Donald Trump at a time when the president's approval ratings were at an all-time low.  

'Despicable betrayal': Haley Stevens endorses Republican candidate over party nominee Abdul El-Sayed
Read More »

Trump has repeatedly called Sayed "a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel", and insisted that he would only call him "Mohammed" because that's what the majority of Muslims are called, Trump said. 

Republicans also cast doubt on his allegiance to the US Constitution, claiming he had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood because of statements his half-sister once made.

There is no known evidence tying Sayed to the group, which has no central hub and was not designated as a terrorist organisation in the US until Trump sanctioned three of its political branches last year. 

Sayed said in August that the focus on his name and identity is "the only play they got" against him. 

"It's like, wow, he's different," he said of Republican attacks.

"That's the best you got? You can't actually talk about what you want to do? My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can't afford your groceries."

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] How the UAE-Israel-Morocco threat pushed Algiers to send troops to Niger
item.description:
How the UAE-Israel-Morocco threat pushed Algiers to send troops to Niger

Submitted by Elis Gjevori on Wed, 11/04/2026 - 08:09
Rival gas projects with Morocco and growing Emirati influence in the Sahel drive Algeria’s move to break with its non-intervention doctrine
Nigerien President Abdourahamane Tiani and Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune at a meeting on 16 February 2026 in Algiers (Algerian Presidency)
Off

An Algerian military convoy arrived in Niger last Friday, marking the country's first deployment of forces abroad since 1973, when it supported Egypt in its war against the Israeli occupation of the Sinai peninsula.

The deployment marks a major departure from Algeria’s longstanding policy of principled non-intervention. It follows Algiers’ decision to send four fighter jets to Niger on 30 August to thwart an attempted coup against President Abdourahamane Tiani.

Although the North African state opposed the 2023 coup that brought Tiani to power, Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune now appears willing to offer the beleaguered leader a much-needed lifeline.

Tiani requested the deployment. Speaking on Sunday, Algerian Senator Belkacem Boulghiti said the troops would protect economic infrastructure and oil facilities belonging to Algerian companies.

Algeria is “not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger”, Boulghiti added.

Retired senior Algerian diplomat Amar Belani offered a clue to Algiers’ thinking in an article published in October.

Belani described growing instability in the Sahel, including Niger, as part of a “destabilisation strategy actively involving the United Arab Emirates, Morocco, Israel and certain French proxies”.

Continuing instability in Niger would “directly threaten Algerian interests” and hinder the Nigeria-Niger-Algeria trans-Saharan gas pipeline project, he added.

Security imperative

Zine Ghebouli, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told Middle East Eye that the situation in the region “is imposing new security imperatives on Algiers and the necessity to secure its strategic interests, particularly in the energy sector”.

This evolving regional situation includes an increasingly strong presence of the United Arab Emirates, with which Algeria severed diplomatic relations in September after “exhausting all means to preserve bilateral relations”.

'Algeria has accused the UAE of being responsible for bloodshed across the region and views the Emirati role as destructive'

- Zine Ghebouli, visiting fellow, ECFR

The Algerian foreign ministry said it had repeatedly warned Abu Dhabi over its “hostile actions”, devoting significant effort to “drawing the attention of the Emirati side and warning it of the grave consequences that may result from its regrettable and unjustified behaviour”.

“Despite these numerous warnings, the United Arab Emirates has persisted in these actions, which have reached a point where they can no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable within the framework of relations between two sovereign states, or remain unanswered,” the statement added.

“The fact that Algiers took the plunge to break relations proves that Emirati manoeuvering was deemed by Algerian authorities as explosive and irreconcilable,” Ghebouli said.

The UAE’s regional interventions and partnership with Israel have drawn growing opposition from governments across the region. Sudan broke ties with Abu Dhabi over its documented funding and fuelling of the country’s bloody civil war.

Somalia, Libya and Yemen have also accused Abu Dhabi of threatening their territorial integrity through its support for rival armed groups and separatist forces.

Analysis: How Algeria came to treat the UAE as a national security threat
Read More »

“For Algiers, Abu Dhabi’s diplomatic, financial and military support to several actors in the region from Libya to Sudan and the Sahel serves divisions,” Ghebouli said.

“Algeria has accused the UAE of being responsible for bloodshed across the region and views the Emirati role as destructive. Also, the Emirati lobbying and pressures on regional actors to expand the Abraham Accords was another point of discord,” he added, referring to the normalisation deals with Israel and Arab states, including Morocco.

In recent years, the UAE has intensively cultivated relationships with the Sahel’s military regimes through high-level diplomacy, gold trading and investment.

In May 2025, Emirati minister Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan met the leaders of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger to discuss cooperation in economic development, energy and other sectors. Mali’s government explicitly included security among the subjects discussed.

“The Sahel has long been considered as an extension of Algerian national security and Algiers now is actively acting based on that,” said Ghebouli.

“Current geopolitical shifts and all that entails in regards to rivalry with and interventions of foreign actors mean that new tools, such as a show of presence including at the military level, are no longer a taboo and will be utilised to draw and reinforce Algeria’s redlines,” he added.

Competing energy corridors

Eastern Libya’s de facto ruler, Khalifa Haftar, presents another concern. The UAE backs Haftar, who commands the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF).

His military expansion towards the corridors connecting Libya and Niger has heightened Algerian concerns about Emirati influence along its southern flank.

'By securing Niger, Algeria is protecting its own answer to the Morocco-UAE axis'

- Dr Fatiha Dazi-Heni, senior political scientist at Irsem 

“Algeria has had a poor relationship with the Haftar family for several years, and the mutiny in Niger in the last days of August illustrated it,” Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst affiliated with the Royal United Services Institute, told MEE.

Haftar’s son Saddam supports Mahamoud Sallah, a Nigerien opponent of Tiani.

“Saddam Haftar and the Algerian state are on opposing sides,” Harchaoui said of Niger.

“That being said, observers mustn’t assume that Algeria is intervening in Libya. Its current effort is to deploy troops on Nigerien soil, so its mission relates to what happens inside Niger: maintaining security within a framework that will become clearer over the coming days and weeks,” he added.

Turkey’s rapprochement with Haftar in October could help Algeria consolidate its foothold in the Sahel. Ankara and Algiers maintain close diplomatic relations and share interests in Libya and Sudan, potentially giving Algeria a back channel to Haftar.

Rabat is also making overtures to the Haftar family, according to reports. Lieutenant General Khaled Haftar, another of Khalifa Haftar’s sons and chief of the general staff of the eastern Libyan forces, paid an official visit to Morocco last month.

The Sahel, a new front in the rivalry between Algeria and Morocco
Read More »

Separately, energy and economic interests also underpin Algeria’s approach to Niger.

Algeria’s national energy company Sonatrach, the Nigerien government and the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation are jointly developing a 4,000-km pipeline to carry Nigerian gas through Niger and Algeria and onwards to Europe.

“The troops are meant to protect energy installations, notably Sonatrach’s oil projects and the corridor of the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline”, said Dr Fatiha Dazi-Heni, a senior political scientist specialising in the Arabian Peninsula at Irsem in Paris and Sciences Po Lille.

Morocco is promoting a rival pipeline along an Atlantic route, drawing on the same Nigerian gas reserves to supply the same European markets.

Crucially, the UAE has agreed to support the Nigeria-Morocco pipeline financially and technically.

“Niger is the one country the overland route cannot bypass. By securing Niger, Algeria is protecting its own answer to the Morocco-UAE axis. Rabat and Abu Dhabi clearly have an interest in the Atlantic route prevailing, and Israel indirectly through its partnership with Morocco,” Dazi-Heni told MEE.

“Algeria’s traditionally cautious strategic culture” now reflects “the new strategic constraints it faces”, she added.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] ‘Complicit’: World Medical Association criticised for rejecting calls to suspend Israel
item.description:
‘Complicit’: World Medical Association criticised for rejecting calls to suspend Israel

Submitted by Amara Sophia Elahi on Wed, 11/04/2026 - 08:11
The WMA maintains Israel's membership despite allegations of Israeli doctors' involvement in torture and complicity in the Gaza genocide
Medics from the IMA Out! campaign protest outside the World Medical Association General Assembly in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, on 10 October 2026 (IMA Out!)
Off

The World Medical Association (WMA) is facing strong criticism for refusing to suspend the Israeli Medical Association (IMA), despite documented allegations of complicity by Israeli doctors in the torture of Palestinian detainees and abuses committed in Gaza.

A petition signed by 6,500 medical personnel from the IMA Out! campaign, a coalition of health advocacy groups, was presented to the WMA General Assembly in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, last month, calling on the international body to expel the IMA.

Hundreds of doctors also took part in protests as the General Assembly was convening, with some carrying a shroud bearing the names of 18,000 Palestinian children who have been killed during Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Doctors argue that the IMA has failed to uphold core standards relating to medical ethics, and that they are complicit in serious violations of human rights against Palestinians, including failing to penalise Israeli doctors who may have overseen the torture of Palestinian detainees and the deaths of Palestinian healthcare workers in Israeli prisons.

The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF), a group seeking justice for war crimes, crimes against humanity and human rights violations committed by Israel against Palestinians, also filed a complaint last month to the International Criminal Court (ICC), urging it to investigate whether Israeli doctors, as well as the IMA and officials from Israel’s ministries of health and defence, have been involved in the torturing of Palestinians.

It is the first time that a WMA member has been referred to the ICC.

Dr Jonathan Fluxman, a retired British GP of Jewish heritage and organising member of the IMA Out! campaign, attended the protests in Rotterdam.

“Both the WMA and IMA are refusing to investigate multiple reports by numerous human rights agencies that were sent directly to them relating to the torture and murder of healthcare workers,” he told Middle East Eye.

“This goes back 30 years - the WMA has been burying reports about Israeli torture.

“They are behaving in the same way as the US and British governments, by allowing Israel to get away with a genocide. In my view, the WMA is complicit in the IMA’s involvement in this.”

‘Carte blanche’ to Israel

Dr Fluxman believes that the WMA should immediately initiate an investigation into the potential involvement of IMA members in the torture, abuse and deaths of Palestinian detainees.

“This is about defending medical principles and the application of them,” he said.

“It raises very serious questions about the WMA’s role as the international guardian of medical ethics, and we understand that a number of national medical associations remain very concerned about the situation.”

‘It raises very serious questions about the WMA’s role as the international guardian of medical ethics’

- Dr Jonathan Fluxman, retired British GP

The WMA was established in 1947 to uphold medical ethics following the Second World War, after doctors from Nazi Germany were found to have participated in war crimes.

One hundred and eighteen countries are currently represented within the international body.

Each member country must adhere to WMA codes of practice, including its 1975 Declaration of Tokyo, which states that doctors must not participate in torture and have a duty to call it out.

The last time an association was suspended was in 1976, when South Africa was blocked from attending two general assemblies due to doctors being complicit in torture during the apartheid.

The first attempt to hold the IMA accountable for the alleged participation of Israeli doctors in the abuse of Palestinian detainees came in 2009, when 725 physicians from 43 countries presented findings by human rights groups to the WMA, which that year was holding its general assembly in Tel Aviv.

At the time, the president of the IMA, Yoram Blachar, was also president of the WMA - he rejected allegations that Israeli medics were complicit in torture, describing them as defamatory.

In 2016, 71 UK-based doctors again urged the WMA to suspend the IMA, but it refused.

The Israeli association represents over 90 percent of doctors in Israel. Its current president, Zion Hagay, chairs the WMA’s socio-medical affairs committee, while its chief executive officer advocate, Leah Wapner, serves in several advisory roles, including on the WMA’s finance and planning, socio-medical affairs, and medical ethics committees.

Dr Fluxman believes that the international body is protecting the IMA.

“What has 30 years of inclusion and dialogue led to? Things have got worse, and the IMA has been given carte blanche to do whatever it wants,” he said.

Around 1,700 healthcare workers have been killed by Israel since October 2023.

South African push to expel IMA

The call for the IMA to be suspended from the WMA was led by the South African Medical Association (Sama) last year.

Sama’s motion failed to secure the majority that was needed to get the WMA to consider expelling the Israeli group. Instead, the WMA passed a resolution calling on the Israeli government to protect healthcare and health workers in Gaza, and asked all its members to issue public statements condemning attacks on hospitals and medical personnel.

The IMA has remained silent on this, however.

Dr Mvuyisi Mzukwa, the chairman of Sama, told MEE his group had decided to take its own approach against the IMA.

“We were the first medical association to formally cut ties with the IMA,” he said.

How the Israeli Medical Association politicised medicine to defend genocide in Gaza
Read More »

This was followed by the British Medical Association and the Turkish Medical Association.

“We also withdrew from the WMA’s Taipei Working Group on ethics because it is chaired by an Israeli medic. It is hugely problematic that the IMA is part of the WMA’s leadership structures, given the allegations surrounding them,” Mzukwa said.

“As a world body, the WMA’s name is being tarnished by the presence of the IMA, and they should have suspended them until these controversies are resolved.

“It is a huge indictment on the WMA. The international body must be clear about the principles it stands for.”

Dr Mzukwa explained that he had been planning to arrive earlier at this year’s General Assembly in order to rally other members of the WMA to join the call for the IMA to be boycotted.

However, he and most of his South African colleagues could not attend because of visa issues.

“I had applied on time, but for some reason the visa ended up being sent to Pretoria rather than Durban, where it usually goes, and there was no way I could have collected it in time for the General Assembly,” he said.

“I have my suspicions about why this might have happened. I was planning to give a speech at the General Assembly and was prepared to put my head above the parapet to call for the IMA to be expelled.

“It’s not beyond the realms of possibility that there could have been some intel on me to try to prevent me from attending.”

MEE contacted the Netherlands’ Ministry of Foreign Affairs for comment but received no response by the time of publication.

Mzukwa has been vocal in his criticism of Israel’s genocide in Gaza. His stance aligns with that of the South African government, which brought a case to the International Court of Justice in 2023 accusing Israel of committing genocide.

Dr Mzukwa also told MEE that Sama, the IMA and the WMA had held a meeting at the end of July about the case of Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, a Palestinian paediatrician and former head of Kamal Adwan Hospital in Gaza, who has been detained by Israel since December 2024 and subjected to brutal beatings.

“We raised concerns about the lack of access to Dr Abu Safiya, the denial of medical treatment for him and uncertainty around his condition,” Dr Mzukwa explained.

“The IMA told us they had requested the Israeli authorities to carry out medical examinations and allow external physicians into the prison where Dr Abu Safiya is being held, but we weren’t shown any evidence to support this - this was a red flag for us.”

‘A buttress of the Israeli state’

Derek Summerfield, an honorary senior lecturer at King’s College London who has researched and campaigned on the psychiatric impact of the detention and torture of Palestinian prisoners in Israel, has been calling on the WMA to expel the Israeli association for almost two decades.

“We’re dealing with two ethically corrupt bodies - the WMA and the IMA - and are appealing to one to do something with the other one - but the WMA has long since sold out,” he told MEE.

‘We’re dealing with two ethically corrupt bodies - the WMA and the IMA - and are appealing to one to do something with the other one - but the WMA has long since sold out’

- Dr Derek Summerfield, King’s College London

“There is a long-established body of evidence on Israeli doctors’ complicity in torture suites, and these days they are even more present there, and participate directly.

“The IMA is an example of the disgusting way in which doctors can behave - they are shielding doctors’ involved in Israel’s genocide on Gaza, and it’s outrageous that they’re a full member of the WMA.

“The IMA really is the buttress of the Israeli state.”

Dr Fluxman has also raised concerns about how the IMA’s ethical policy allows for exemptions from the WMA’s principles.

“It is their policy to allow Israeli doctors to compromise fundamental ethical principles and defer to military and security officials over the provision of healthcare and protection of health personnel,” he said.

“It also means they are in breach of the WMA’s position on medical neutrality.”

The IMA has consistently remained silent amid ongoing attacks on healthcare facilities in Gaza, as well as the targeting of healthcare workers.

In fact, it has frequently sought to challenge criticism of Israel’s actions by international medical associations.  

Palestinian bodies released by Israel came from infamous Sde Teiman detention centre
Read More »

At this year’s WMA General Assembly, the IMA installed banners outside the convention, calling on medical associations not to boycott them and asking them to remember the 7 October 2023 attacks.

In November 2023, IMA’s president, Professor Hagay, refused to call for a ceasefire and justified Israeli military strikes on hospitals in Gaza, arguing that Hamas fighters needed to be “rooted out of terror bases”.

That month, 81 Israeli doctors signed a letter supporting the bombing of hospitals, something which the IMA refused to condemn, contravening WMA principles on the protection of healthcare settings and health workers.

Furthermore, Dr Liav Goldstein, a senior member of the IMA’s ethics bureau and chief medical officer of the Israeli Prison Service, has approved the starvation diet imposed on thousands of Palestinian prisoners after 7 October by the national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir.

The IMA’s attempts to safeguard the reputation of the Israeli state were also laid bare when in May 2024, Hagay wrote to the Israeli Prison Service about the death in prison of Dr Adnan al-Bursh, a Palestinian surgeon who was head of the orthopaedic department at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.

After a highly critical British Medical Journal article about the circumstances surrounding Dr Al-Bursh's death, Professor Hagay wrote: “We would appreciate any information that could help us refute this claim, which, needless to say, causes significant harm to Israel’s standing and image worldwide.”

Torture camp

Whistleblowers from Sde Teiman, an Israeli military base in the Negev desert that was converted into a detention camp at the start of the Gaza genocide, have documented the systemic abuse and torture of Palestinian detainees there, including the denial of medical treatment by Israeli medics.

Accounts describe prisoners being held naked, shackled and forced to wear nappies instead of being allowed to use a toilet.

Some have also had to undergo amputations, often without anaesthesia.

'The WMA must answer why an association that provided institutional cover for torture is still welcome at its table'

- Dyab Abou Jahjah, Hund Rajab Association

The centre has been used to detain thousands of Palestinians from Gaza, the majority of whom are civilians, including healthcare and humanitarian workers, who are being held under the so-called “unlawful combatants” law, which has been used to strip detainees of basic legal protections and enable their detention without charge or trial.

Several individuals have died while being held there.

IMA ethics board director Yossi Walfisch dismissed accusations of ill-treatment and said prisoners at the camp were receiving “appropriate medical care”.

Dr Al-Bursh was held at Sde Teiman before being taken to Ofer Prison, where he died. While in prison he was brutally beaten, tortured and repeatedly raped, according to testimonies of released Palestinian prisoners who had met him.

The Hind Rajab Foundation said evidence shows that medical participation in torture and abuse at the camp was structural.

Dyab Abou Jahjah, director general at HRF, said: “Israeli physicians abandoned their neutrality when they agreed to treat patients in chains and erase what was done to them.

“The WMA must answer why an association that provided institutional cover for torture is still welcome at its table.”

If IMA members are found to be complicit in this, it would violate the WMA’s code of practice, values and guidelines, as well as international humanitarian law, Abou Jahjah said.

The WMA told MEE: “Inclusion sits at the core of the WMA's identity. Patients remain our focus, alongside the protection of health personnel, including physicians, wherever they serve.

“Our members, including the Israeli Medical Association, regularly call out injustices and violations of medical neutrality even when their own governments are involved.”

MEE also contacted IMA but received no response by the time of publication.

Israel's Shin Bet arrests activist amid incitement over Palestinian electoral gains

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 11/04/2026 - 08:33
Abu Shahadeh's detention comes amid accusations that Netanyahu’s government is seeking to undermine election results following a strong turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel
Abu Shahadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, was arrested by masked officers who stormed his house at midnight (Provided)
Off

Israeli security forces arrested prominent Palestinian political activist and journalist Abd Abu Shahadeh on Tuesday, amid incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel following their historic electoral gains in last week’s elections.

Abu Shahadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, was taken from his home in Jaffa around midnight and transferred to an undisclosed location, according to news outlet Arab48.

Around 15 security personnel, including masked officers, stormed the house, arresting Abu Shahadeh in front of his two children. They also seized electronic devices and several books.

Police confirmed that the case was under investigation by the Tel Aviv Central Unit and Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic intelligence agency. A court subsequently issued a publication ban, citing a “security-related investigation”.

Abd Abu Shahadeh heads the elected Islamic Council in Jaffa and is a member of the editorial board of the Arab 48 news website. He is also a regular contributor to Middle East Eye’s opinion section.

The arrest comes amid a wave of incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel following their record voter turnout and electoral gains in last week’s elections.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party claimed the elections had been “stolen” by Palestinian parties, citing allegations of foreign interference.

Opposition figures have accused Likud of attempting to undermine the election results by exaggerating the allegations.

Palestinian-led parties denied the accusations.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee certified the election results on Wednesday, saying it had found no evidence of irregularities that undermined the integrity of the election or affected the outcome.

on Tuesday, Shin Bet chief David Zini, an ally of Netanyahu, was seeking to question the leaders of Palestinian-led parties under caution.

One source pointed to Zini’s declaration on election day that the vote was secure.

The allegations emerged after Palestinian-led parties won a record 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset, dealing a major blow to Netanyahu’s coalition.

The prime minister’s bloc won 53 seats, down from 64 in the 2022 elections, leaving him unable to form a majority government with the same parties. The opposition bloc also fell short of the numbers needed to secure a majority, resulting in political deadlock.

Aipac and the Michigan Senate race: How the Israel lobby became toxic

"A lobby is like a night flower: it thrives in the dark and dies in the sun.” So said Steve Rosen, former foreign policy director of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) in a memo to a fellow staffer. Rosen would later be fired amid a major scandal involving espionage in passing classified US information to Israel. 

Rosen was correct about the danger to a lobbying organisation that publicity poses. But in December 2021, Aipac decided to test that theory by creating two political action committees (Pacs) that enabled it to take part directly in political campaigns.

The results were mixed, and Aipac recently announced that it was closing one of the Pacs it had set up. 

Aipac had been an advocacy organisation, promoting Israel’s interests, but it did not fund campaigns directly, nor did it endorse or fund political candidates. 

In many ways, that made it more effective. It could do things like issue a congressional report card which rated every member of Congress’s support of Israel. Then other groups that were actual Pacs could use those reports to decide which candidates they should be contributing to.

‘Israel cannot afford to ignore’: Israeli press reels from Democratic sweep

The Israeli press is taking stock of last night’s Democratic sweep of Congress, sounding the alarm over the consequences for Israel.

A Haaretz analysis this morning said Abdul El-Sayed’s victory over pro-Israel candidate Mike Rogers demonstrated “that even strident opposition to Israel is no barrier to winning competitive federal races.”

“El-Sayed won despite AIPAC spending more than $30 million to defeat him in the Democratic primary and another reported $9 million on behalf of Rogers in the general election,” it added.

The Jerusalem Post warned: “The implications of the US midterm elections for Israel could extend far beyond the loss of Republican control of Congress. The defeat comes amid broader shifts within the Democratic Party regarding Israel, the war with Iran, and the strategic relationship between Jerusalem and Washington.”

“One of the clearest takeaways from the election campaign is the political price the war with Iran has exacted on the Republican Party”, the analysis said, referring to the war Israel pushed the US into on 28 February.

“The expansion of the camp critical of Israel, and its growing access to positions of influence, represents a shift that Israel cannot afford to ignore,” it added.
